name: The Lantern Causeway
unique_feature: a boardwalk of lantern poles over the wet lit each dusk by a lamplighter who sings as she goes, a rope run from pole-top to pole-top, and at its Isseva end her hut, her ladder against the first pole and her long wick-pole
story: The lamplighter Lissane has walked it for forty years. When she is late the boardwalk is not safe, and she is late on purpose when she wants Isseva to notice her.
encounter: bog-drowned climb the poles after dark if the lanterns are out

name: Drowned Bell Shrine
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on a peat island above a bell that tolls once at midnight from under the water
story: The reedfolk bury their dead with lanterns; the bell is older than any of them and nobody buried it.
encounter: none; wisps circle at midnight

name: The Sallow King
unique_feature: a willow so old its branches have rooted again in a ring, making a hall of trunks
story: Sallowjaws nest under its roots and the reedfolk feed them so they nest nowhere else. It is the only place in the marsh where you are asked not to kill anything.
encounter: sallowjaw ambush from the water inside the ring; a moral choice with reputation cost

name: The Reed Wreck
unique_feature: a Salt Isles trading ship stranded three miles inland, sitting nearly upright in the reeds with the reeds grown up through her, her mast standing with its yard and shrouds, her deckhouse door swung open, a crate with a chart on it under her bow
story: No flood on record could have carried it here. The reedfolk say the Tide came in once, briefly, and went out again; the ship's log stops the day before.
encounter: leech-hounds in the hold; a chart of the Salt Isles

name: The Stair of Isse
unique_feature: a sunken Oroth colonnade rising step by step out of the water toward the Drowned Nave
story: The Builders' processional way. The reedfolk call it Isse's Stair and say the Named woman walked down it into the water to teach the stilts.
encounter: bog-drowned rise from between the columns as you pass; fight on the steps, not in the water

name: Wisp Hollow
unique_feature: a dead-end channel where wisps gather over a drowned house whose chimney still stands
story: The family's lanterns were never lit for them; the wisps are what a water-burial becomes when nobody sings.
encounter: wisps lure toward deep water; silence them or ignore their light; a strongbox in the chimney

name: The Tideflat Stones
unique_feature: three stones in a line at the sea's edge marking a shoreline that is no longer there, the first on the flats, the second in the shallows, the third out in the water; the facing stones of an old quay along where the shore was, and the western chart's survey-cairn with its pole and rag
story: The soft western edge. Beyond them the flats go grey and the Salt Isles are a rumour. A survey point for the western chart.

name: Heron Watch
unique_feature: a reedfolk lookout on tall braced stilts over the channel, a bell-cote on its ridge where a bittern nests in the bell, and the keeper's knotted bell-rope hanging all the way down to the stair's foot
story: The watch was raised to see the Lakefolk coming for the weir. Now it is where young reedfolk go to be alone together.
encounter: none; a vista over the delta

name: The Fog Bell
unique_feature: a tall timber bell-frame on stilts by the channel, its bell under a little reed roof and its rope run down to the ringer's hut at the foot, a landing stage out into the channel with a lantern on its end post
story: The ringer is paid in eels by Moreva and Isseva both, and rings through the night whenever the fog is in, which is most nights. When the bell stops, the boats come in to find out why.
encounter: since the ringer went, the drowned come up the landing at night and stand at his open door
hook: The Fog Bell stopped last night, and the ringer is not in the tower.

name: The Long Jetty
unique_feature: a burial boardwalk running out into Lissane Mere, its posts knotted with the knots of the unmourned and its last post hung thick with lanterns, a name painted on each
story: Isseva buries its own from the town jetty. The Long Jetty is for the drowned who come up without a name; the reedfolk light a lantern for each and sing the third voice of the round.
encounter: bog-drowned climb to the last post at midnight
hook: Somebody has been leaving lanterns with names on them at the Long Jetty, and the names are all from the Vale.

name: The Peat Hags
unique_feature: a peat-cutters' camp on a drying island: the cutting-bank stepped down in three cuts with black water in its floor, the turves stacked to dry in rows of little pyramids like loaves, the cutters' reed hut and fire, and the finds-board where what the peat gives up is laid out for the buyers
story: Peat from the south marsh warms Isseva, Nauve's Landing and half of Tollmere's poorer streets. The cutters find things in the peat, and are paid more for the finding than for the peat.
encounter: leech-hounds come up to the cuttings after dark
hook: The cutters have dug up a Warden, perfectly kept, with a roll of names in his hand; the Wardens and the Order both want him.

name: The Drowned Arch
unique_feature: one arch of the Builders' black stone standing at the edge of Mormere with nothing on either side of it, the mere lapping in under it, its keystone hung with eel-boat luck-knots, the stones of the wall it stood in lying sunk in the reeds either side
story: The reedfolk say the arch was a door and the marsh was a room. Eel-boats pass under it for luck, and never through it the other way.
encounter: none
hook: An eel-boat went through the Drowned Arch the wrong way and came out at dawn with its crew a day older than they should be.

name: The Sunken Tower
unique_feature: a Builders' tower of black fused stone drowned to its third course in a black mere, its fourth course carved round with a face that looks out to sea, a children's diving plank off its broken top and the drowned courses of its outer wall a ring of stones awash round it
story: Once a watch over a shore that is a mile out to sea now. The children dive from the top to touch the fourth course, which is carved with a face.
encounter: sallowjaws bask on the drowned courses of the outer wall
hook: The face carved on the fourth course is the face of the Thirteenth colossus.

name: The Traders' Post
unique_feature: the beach where Salt Isles traders drew up their boats: the bare frames of their tents still standing in a row along the strand, one tent put up again by Oulea for the longest day with a trader's chart pinned to its pole, the keel-grooves of their boats running down to the water
story: The traders came every midsummer for three hundred years and stopped forty years ago without a word. Oulea still puts up one tent for them on the longest day.
encounter: none
hook: This midsummer a trader's chart was pinned to a tent-pole, and there was no boat on the sea.

name: The Eel-Boat Graveyard
unique_feature: eel-boats left to rot on the flats where the reedfolk say the drowned come ashore to count them
story: A reedfolk boat is never broken up; when it is done it is brought here and left to the tide. There are three hundred of them, and some of them have moved in the night.
encounter: bog-drowned walk among the hulls at night
hook: Ollo Nauve built one of the boats that moved, and wants it back where he left it.

name: Crookstilts
unique_feature: a hut on stilts that each lean their own way in the carr, cords knotted with names hung under its deck, the marsh-hag's price chalked on a slate at the foot of its stair beside the flat stone where you stand to say a name
story: The marsh-hag the reedfolk call the Name-Wife comes up to Crookstilts at the dark of the moon and cures anything, and takes in payment a name you know, never your own. The rest of the month the stilts stand empty with the cords hanging under them, waiting to be carried south to her hollow under the scarp. The reedfolk go to her anyway, and do not say whose names they gave.
encounter: her leech-hounds guard the stilts after dark
hook: The marsh-hag has Tessane's name, and will trade it.

name: The Indigo Beds
unique_feature: Isseva's north dye beds: long reed troughs of steeping indigo in rows, the liquor near-black in all of them but the row nearest the Nave, which has gone pale; cloth drying on lines between
story: The only indigo in Wickmere comes up in these beds. This year it is coming up pale, and the dyers blame the fog, and Loa Oul blames the drowned.
encounter: none; dyers with jobs going
hook: Find out where the indigo's colour is going: the dyers have noticed the pale beds are the ones nearest the Nave.

name: The Round Stones
unique_feature: three stones on three peat islets in black water, a long stone's throw apart, where the Round of Sa'oul is sung at midsummer, a choir on each: the singers' reed mats in a crescent round each stone, facing the next
story: The round goes from stone to stone across the water, each voice starting as the last reaches the third line. It does not end; somebody stops, and then somebody else.
encounter: none by day; at night wisps sing the round's first voice over the water, very nearly right
hook: Sing the second voice slightly flat on the fourth line and an old woman on the far islet begins to weep.

name: Mor'oul
unique_feature: a stilt-village sunk in a flood nobody recorded: black water over all of it, the ridges of its roofs and the tops of its stilts and lantern poles just breaking the surface, and under the water its own lanterns still lit
story: The reedfolk put the drowned's apostrophe into its name the year it went under. The Tide account says a flood; there has never been a flood in any record, except here, in the name.
encounter: bog-drowned at their own doors
hook: Under the water Mor'oul's own lanterns are still lit.

name: Oskel Ford
unique_feature: an Oroth footbridge of column-drums laid across the Oskel where it comes down out of the heights into the fen, and in the fen beside it an ore-cart run off the crossing and left with its silver still in it, the carters' boots in the mud
story: The only dry way from the clans' Oskeld Dale into the fen. Oskel miners carry lead down it to trade at Isseva, and the reedfolk never cross it the other way.
encounter: whatever took the carters comes back to the cart at night
hook: Ore-carts have been found in the fen with the silver still aboard and the carters gone, and the Oskel clan want the ford watched.

name: Saoul
unique_feature: a ring of a dozen empty stilts standing in a black pool, the platform they held long gone, a lit lantern hung from a hook on every one, and at the pool's edge a shrine-post hung with Saeva's knots
story: The lantern-pool, named for Sa'oul, who is in it. The village that stood here moved to Saeva a hundred years ago and left its lanterns for her.
encounter: wisps over the pool at night
hook: The lanterns are relit every night, and the reedfolk swear that none of them does it.

name: The Greyreed Decoy
unique_feature: a wildfowlers' decoy in the reeds: a black pool with three netted pipes curving off it under hoops of withy, wattle screens staggered along each, the decoyman's hut, and at the end of one pipe the net torn open from inside
story: Nauvissa's decoyman draws the Greyreed's ducks up the netted pipes with a dog and a song. He sells every bird to Tollmere and eats none of them.
encounter: none; a decoyman and his dog
hook: The decoy dog has started leading something else up the pipes at night, and the nets are torn from inside.

name: The Salt Pans
unique_feature: square brine pools in rows behind clay banks on the tideflats, the near ones wet and the far ones drying white, the rakers' huts on legs and the salt heaped under reed; one pan crusted overnight with a line of bare footprints across it from the sea side and none coming back
story: The only salt in Wickmere that is not carried down from the Skerrow mines. The reedfolk trade it for lamp-oil and say the sea is giving back what it owes.
encounter: none; salt-rakers
hook: A pan dried to a crust overnight with footprints across it from the sea side, and none coming back.

name: The Tide Hearth
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on the Outfall's south bank hung round with lantern-knots, one for every name the water has taken, facing the Saltgate's walls across the water; beside it a sluice-hand's shelter of sail over two oars and a line of twelve knots for the Saltgate's watch
story: Reedfolk who have lost someone to the water come here to tie a knot and say the name once. The Sayers call it superstition; the Tallymen charge nothing to pass it, which is the most respect Tollmere has. Since the autumn a Guild sluice-hand has sat by it under a sail, learning the knots from the people who come to tie them, so that he can tie one for each of his watch.
encounter: none; Hal Ruddock keeps to the bank
hook: A knot has been tied for a name nobody in Sedgemire knows, and it stays dry in the spray.

name: The Old Crannog
unique_feature: an island-house older than any stilt in Sedgemire: a heap of stones raised in a black pool of the carr, on it a round house of wattle under a cone of reed, a fire laid ready at its door and a causeway of stones and logs out to the bank, three of them loose
story: The reedfolk say their grandmothers' grandmothers lived on islands before Isse taught them stilts. The crannog is the last one, and nobody sleeps in it twice.
encounter: leech-hounds in the carr at night
hook: Somebody has been sleeping in it every night, and leaves the fire laid for the next.

name: The Knuckle Cairn
unique_feature: a clan cairn on a rise of grey rock, the last dry stone before the fen, capped with a giant's knuckle-bone turned to point into the fen; the clans' sign-cords on stakes round it and a lead-carrier's offering of lead pigs at its foot
story: The Oskel clan's boundary. Past it, the clans say, is not their memory's business.
encounter: none; at night leech-hounds come up out of the fen as far as the stakes and no further
hook: The knuckle-bone has been turned to point into the fen, which in clan sign means follow.

name: The Drowned Road
unique_feature: an Oroth road of fused black slabs running dead straight out of the carr and down into the sea, its kerbs either side, its last slabs under the water, and out in the shallows past its end a milestone cut with a number
story: The Builders' road west, cut off where the sea took the land. The reedfolk say it goes on under the water to the Salt Isles, and the Salt Isles traders say it arrives.
encounter: sallowjaws lie along the drowned slabs
hook: At the lowest tide this spring the road showed a milestone further out than anyone had seen, cut with a number.

name: The Grey Gull
unique_feature: a Salt Isles trading ship driven onto the carr's edge and lying hard over on her side, her mast snapped and fallen along the shingle, and under her bowsprit her figurehead: a gull with swept wings and a woman's face staring up the carr
story: She came ashore in the storm of 1031 with nobody aboard and her boats still lashed. The reedfolk have taken nothing from her, because a ship that comes without its crew has come for someone.
encounter: none
hook: The figurehead's face has been recognised: a reedfolk woman of Moreva, alive, who has never been to sea.

name: The Boardwalk Gate
unique_feature: a reedfolk gate of two tall posts and a lintel hung with lanterns and indigo cloth where the Westway leaves the downs and goes onto a boardwalk over the delta, and on the boardwalk's planks wet prints of bare feet coming out of the delta
story: Nauvissa keeps the gate and lights it every dusk, so that the Vale's carters know where the ground stops.
encounter: none
hook: The lanterns were found lit at noon, and the boardwalk wet with footprints coming out of the delta.

name: The Reed Bridge
unique_feature: a footbridge of bundled reed over a creek, a new one laid on the old every spring
story: Nobody has taken the old bridge down in two hundred years; the reedfolk lay the new one on top, and the bridge stands higher every year.
encounter: none
hook: The bridge has sunk to the water overnight, two hundred years of reed pressed flat as if something very heavy had crossed.

name: The Eel Hurdles
unique_feature: the eel-trappers' summer raft moored on the channel, two reed huts on a deck of logs, and out from it in the black water three long vees of wattle hurdles steering the eels into the traps at their points
story: Oulea's trappers live out on the water from thaw to first frost and come ashore only for burials.
encounter: none; eel-trappers
hook: Every morning the traps are full of eels swimming the wrong way, out to sea.

name: The Cockle Beds
unique_feature: the tideflats' cockle-beds staked out in family rows, each stake tied with its family's knot in indigo, rush or red, every stake moved one row toward the sea in the night with its old hole plain in the mud behind it; shell heaps by the sorting board
story: The reedfolk rake the beds at low water. A stake moved in the night has started more feuds in Sedgemire than eels have.
encounter: none by day; at the night's low water the drowned come up the rows to the stakes
hook: Every stake on the beds was found moved one row toward the sea.

name: The Withy Beds
unique_feature: osier-beds cut to stools in long rows, this year's withies standing up out of each, bundles cut and stacked by the block; at the east end the stools trodden flat and the withies broken where the old bitch's pack lies up by day
story: Nauve's Landing weaves every eel-trap in Sedgemire from these withies, and the beds are older than the Landing.
encounter: none; withy-cutters
hook: The withies have grown a yard since the new moon, and every one of them has grown toward the Mere.

name: The South Stilts
unique_feature: a reedfolk watch-house on tall braced stilts on a shelf of the South Scarp, its stair climbing toward the scarp's lip where the grey sits, a knot-rail along its porch and a cold beacon basket on a pole beside it
story: Nauvissa raised it in the Ash Winter to see the grey coming over the scarp, and for twenty years the grey sat on the lip like fog that had forgotten how to move. This spring it comes down at night, a little way, like a tide, and goes back by morning. The watchman ties a knot on the rail for every night it moves, and nobody in Nauvissa believes him.
encounter: none; Iffo Nauve keeps the watch from dusk
hook: The watchman says the grey has started coming in at night and going back by day, and nobody believes him; he says it started the night after he went to Crookstilts.

name: The Eel Stews
unique_feature: six square stone-walled ponds in the fen where live eels are kept for the Tollmere market, plank walks between them; the sixth walled higher than the rest, its sluice-board down, empty, its wall wet on the outside and two drag-marks running from it to the channel
story: Nauve's Landing sells its eels alive: a dead eel is a Tallyman's price and a live one is a reedfolk's.
encounter: at night sallowjaws come up the drag-marks to the stews
hook: The high-walled pond has been found empty with its sluice shut, and its wall is wet on the outside.

name: The Lantern-Wright's Camp
unique_feature: a reedfolk lantern-maker's camp on a peat hummock beside the Westway, horn panes drying on a rack by the fire
story: Every lantern hung on the Boardwalk Gate and every lantern sunk with the reedfolk's dead is made here, from horn scraped thin enough to read through. The lantern-wright sings rounds while she works, alone, taking every part herself.
encounter: wisps gather at the drying racks after dark, drawn by the horn panes
hook: Every lantern made here this month has come out with its flame burning downward, toward the water.

name: The Lead-Carriers' Rest
unique_feature: a lead-carriers' stopping place at the edge of the fen below Oskel Ford, pack frames stacked beside the fire and a lantern pole marking the dry path
story: Oskel miners carry their lead down out of the dale to trade at Isseva, and rest here before the fen. The reedfolk never cross the ford the other way, and the miners never ask them to; the rest is the one place both stand.
encounter: leech-hounds come up the fen edge at dusk
hook: The reedfolk have started leaving a lantern lit on the pole for the Oskel carriers, which the reedfolk do for nobody who is not drowned.

name: The Drowned Byre
unique_feature: the roofless stone byre of a farm the fen came up over, its long walls broken to the knee and one gable standing whole out of the reeds of the Carr, the manger still along the back wall
story: There was dry pasture on this edge of the fen before the Mere fell and the delta spread, and a clan family kept cattle here, the only clan folk who ever farmed on the flat. The fen came up a hand a year until the byre stood in it, and they drove the beasts up the dale and never came back down.
encounter: bog-drowned climb out of the Carr after dark
hook: Cattle have been heard lowing in the byre at night, and in the morning there is fresh dung on a floor the water has covered for forty years.

name: The Lantern Hummock
unique_feature: a peat island shrine by the North Channel causeway, lantern poles round a stone and an old bell just under the water beside it
story: The reedfolk bury their dead in the water with a lantern. For the ones the water took and did not give back, there is no burial, so a lantern is lit for them here on the hummock, on the one night each year that it can be seen from Moreva.
encounter: none
hook: A lantern has been lit on the hummock for somebody who is still alive, and the reedfolk will not say whose.

name: The Settled House
unique_feature: the stilt-house of a Moreva family whose stilts rotted under it: the house come down whole onto the peat and settled askew, its roof slid half off, the stumps of its stilts standing round it
story: When a stilt-house's stilts rot the reedfolk do not rebuild it. They say the house has come down to meet the water, and the family moves, and the house is left to wait for the flood the Tide account promises. The family's eel-spear lies across the beams, where they can reach it if the water comes before they are ready.
encounter: bog-drowned climb onto the beams after dark
hook: The family has come back to live in it, sitting up on the gable and the beams, waiting, they say, for the water to come up and take them out to where it went.

name: The Pushers' Stones
unique_feature: three leaning stones on the bank below the Eelweir, where whoever was pushed off the weir each autumn climbs out and leans to dry
story: Reedfolk and Lakefolk share the Eelweir by an agreement neither side has read, and every autumn one of them pushes one of the other into the Outfall. The stones are where the pushed climb out and lean, dripping, and are handed a cup by the pusher, which is also the agreement.
encounter: none
hook: This autumn nobody was pushed in, for the first time in anyone's memory, and both sides are frightened of what that means.

name: The Broken Stilts
unique_feature: a ring of stilts snapped off at every height beside the Isseva causeway where a platform stood, the platform's last bearer lying across two of them, the water round them black and still
story: A reedfolk family's fishing platform stood here until a sallowjaw took the stilts out from under it one at a time. The reedfolk did not rebuild. They say the sallowjaw waited forty years for the platform to be worth taking, and has earned the ring.
encounter: a sallowjaw waits in the black water by the stilts
hook: The broken stilts have been found capped with lit lanterns, one for each of the family who lived on the platform, though none of them died there.

name: The Drowned Road Post
unique_feature: a tall lantern pole with indigo rags on the North Fen's safe way to the Drowned Road, its lantern kept lit at dusk
story: The fen round the Drowned Road will take a walker who strays a stride off the hard ground, so the reedfolk mark the safe way with lantern poles, and this is the last before the old road. Its lantern is lit at dusk by whoever passes last.
encounter: none
hook: The lantern has been found lit at dusk and burning under the water, a stride off the safe way, where no hand could have set it.

name: The Peat-Cutters' Light
unique_feature: a lantern pole hung with indigo rags on the Delta's peat, marking the cutters' way home through the fog
story: The peat-cutters work the hags out on the Delta where the fog comes down in an hour, and walk home by the lantern poles. This is the pole the whole way is counted from: from here the Landing's lights can be seen.
encounter: none
hook: The cutters came home through the fog last week and counted one pole more on the way than there has ever been.

name: The Eel-Smoker's Hut
unique_feature: a cone of poles thatched with reed on the Delta's edge by the Westway, smoke seeping through its thatch where eels are hung to cure
story: An old reedfolk woman smokes eels in a reed hut on the dry edge of the Delta, where the Vale's carters meet the boardwalk, and sells them to both sides at one price, which she says is the only fair thing on the Westway.
encounter: none
hook: She has started smoking eels for somebody who comes at night and pays in the Vale's old pennies, the kind with the Toll whole on them.

name: The Drowned Trader
unique_feature: a trading ship sunk to her rails in the Delta's mud beside the Saeva road, black water lying on her deck, her mast leaning far over with indigo rags tied to its shrouds, her lantern on a pole in the mud at her bow
story: A Lakefolk trader came up the Delta too far on a spring tide and settled in the mud when it ran out. The reedfolk tied indigo to her shrouds to mark her for the boats, and say that what went down with her crew still keeps her.
encounter: the drowned rise from the hull after dark
hook: The indigo rags on the shrouds have been untied in the night and tied again in the Lakefolk's knot.

name: The Unsung Vault
unique_feature: a black Oroth doorway sunk to its lintel in a peat hummock of the carr, its approach lined with lantern poles whose lanterns are all cold
story: The Builders cut a cistern under the carr and the carr grew over it. When the reedfolk found it they gave it the drowned nobody could sing for: the ones who came up nameless, the ones whose people were all gone. Their lanterns were carried down and kept lit by a Keeper who sang the whole round for all of them, every night, one Keeper after another for three hundred years. This winter the singing under the carr stopped, and the lanterns on the poles went out one by one from the door outward.
encounter: the drowned wait on the steps of the doorway after dark; inside, the unsung who were never sung for, and the last Keeper at the bottom, still holding her lantern
hook: A knot-cord hangs from the lintel in the Keepers' weave: one knot for every Keeper, and the last knot has been tied and then pulled half undone.

site.hook_prompt: Read the knot-cord on the lintel

name: Greylag Fold
unique_feature: a round withy fold on a dry rise of the North Fen full of grey geese, the goose-herd's stilt-house beside it and her punt drawn up under it
story: The Mors have wintered the grey geese on the North Fen since before the Nave leaned. The geese come down from the clans' country in the first frost and the family brings them in to the fold at dusk by singing, because a goose will follow a round it has heard since the egg. Since the singing under the carr stopped, the geese will not settle; they face west all night, toward the Vault, and call.
encounter: leech-hounds come up out of the carr after the geese at night
hook: The old goose-herd sits up all night on her deck with a lantern, singing the third voice of the round, because, she says, somebody has to.

name: The Stakes at Oulnauve
unique_feature: a palisade of black bog-oak stakes on a peat island where the deep channel bends, its yard heaped with burial lanterns cut from the water, every one unlit
story: The Tide account says the water went out and will come back, and that when it does the drowned will walk ashore. The Flood-Callers are the reedfolk who got tired of waiting for it. They cut the burial lanterns off the water before they can burn down, so that the dead go out with nothing to steer by and come back up, and they call each one that rises a wave of the flood. They have built their stakes where the Oulnauve channel bends, and they have a great many lanterns.
encounter: Flood-Callers on the fighting step and the watch platforms; the Caller, Aunsa Mor, in the yard among the lanterns, and the drowned they have raised penned in the ditch
hook: A burial lantern nailed to the gate by its frame, and on the frame, in fresh indigo, the Callers' mark: a wave, and under it the words THEY ARE COMING HOME.

site.hook_prompt: Look at the lantern nailed to the gate

name: The Eel Tally
unique_feature: a Tallymen's counting-house on stilts at the head of the stews' channel, the Guild's brass lantern over the door and the eel-barrels ranked below it in chalked rows
story: Every live eel that goes up to Tollmere from the Delta is counted at the Tally first, and one in ten stays behind as the Guild's. The reedfolk pole their catch in, the clerk chalks it on the barrels and in the book, and a hired bravo sits on the steps with his hand on his hilt in case anybody counts differently. The clerk this year is new, and he has noticed that the book and the barrels do not agree.
encounter: the Guild's bravo sits on the tally-house steps by day and fights anyone who touches the barrels
hook: One row of barrels has been chalked twice, in two hands, and the numbers do not match.

name: Hester's House
unique_feature: a Vale cottage of lime-washed wattle and thatch set down on a peat island in the reeds, with a barley patch no bigger than a boat and a row of named lanterns on its fence
story: Hester Wrenn came down the Westway from Gosford forty years ago behind a reedman who had come up it selling eels, and he built her a house the way they build them in the Vale so that she would stay. He went into the water twenty years ago and she stayed anyway. She is the only person in Sedgemire who grows barley and the only one who knows the names of the Vale folk the marsh has drowned, because they come to her door first.
encounter: none; a widow who talks to strangers, and a fence of lanterns
hook: One lantern on her fence has no name on it, and she will not say whose it is until somebody asks.

name: Isse's Chair
unique_feature: a ring of nine black stilts of bog-oak, turned to stone at the foot, round a low seat of green Oroth stone heaped with cut reeds and knots
story: The reedfolk say these are the legs of Isse's own house, the first ever built on stilts, and that the seat is where she sat to teach the others how. Couples are married standing between two of the stilts with a reed held between them; the dead are named here before they are sent out. The stilts are older than Isseva, and the seat is Builders' work older than that, and nobody can say who put the one inside the other.
encounter: none; the Chair's tender, and what people leave
hook: Somebody has left a knot on the seat tied in no weave any lantern-maker knows, and it has not rotted in a month of rain.

name: The Leech-Wife's Stilts
unique_feature: a stilt-house over a ring of sunken leech-tubs and empty wattle kennels, a pole of iron collars hung by the door
story: Illa Nauve keeps the leeches Isseva's bleeders use, and she kept the hounds that were bred to guard them: sleek marsh dogs that learned from the leeches how to drink. Last spring the hounds went into the reeds after her old bitch and did not come back, and now they come back every night, and hunt the tubs, and her.
encounter: leech-hounds circle the tubs after dark, the old bitch that leads them among them
hook: The collar pole has one hook empty and scratched bright, as if something had been pulling at it from below.

name: The Draining Mill
unique_feature: a Tollmere windmill with torn sails standing on the open delta, built to pump the marsh dry, its sluice gate choked with reeds and black water
story: Forty years ago the Tallymen bought the rights to the west Delta from the Reed Council for a boat of silver and built a wind-pump to drain it for sheep. It pumped for one summer. The water it lifted out of the ground was not the marsh's water, the Oulea folk say, but something older from underneath, and the engineer went down into the sump to see why it tasted of iron, and the mill has not turned since.
encounter: bog-drowned rise from the sump after dark and walk the dry channel the mill cut
hook: The engineer's pumping-book is still on the ledge by the sluice, open at the last day, with a column of figures that goes wrong halfway down.

name: The Drylanders' Hummock
unique_feature: a low green hummock west of Isseva crowded with earth graves, each marked with a board in a stranger's letters and, beside it, a reedfolk lantern pole
story: The reedfolk give their dead to the water. People from the dry country do not want to go into the water, and say so, and Isseva has always listened: the Tallymen's clerks, the Vale carters, a Warden or two and a Salt Isles sailor are buried here in the earth the way they asked. The reedfolk did not know what else a grave wanted, so each one has a lantern as well.
encounter: wisps come to the lanterns at midnight, when nobody from the dry country is there to light them
hook: The newest board is a Vale name, cut last month, and there is nobody under it.

name: The Bog-Iron Bloomery
unique_feature: a squat clay furnace smoking on a hummock among flooded ore-pits, heaps of rust-red bog ore and charcoal round it and the slag in black rivers down the bank
story: The only iron the reedfolk have is the iron the marsh makes: red ore that grows in the pits a hand's depth a lifetime. The Lissas dig it and smelt it here in a clay bloomery they build again every spring, and every eel-spear and boat-nail in the Delta came out of it. The pits they dug when their grandmothers were girls have filled with water again, and the sallowjaws have found them warm from the furnace.
encounter: sallowjaws lie in the flooded ore-pits and come up at whoever walks the pit edges
hook: The bloomer's tally-cord hangs from the furnace with this spring's blooms knotted on it, and it stops a month ago.

name: The Grey Line
unique_feature: rows of withy stakes driven across the reed-beds south of Nauvissa, one row for every year, each tagged with a knot; beyond the last row the reeds are the colour of ash
story: Every midsummer since the Ash Winter, Nauvissa has walked south to where the reeds go grey and driven a row of stakes along the edge of it, and tied that year's knot to each one. There are sixty rows. The oldest are far in the grey now, their knots gone white; the newest is a reed-bed from the village. Nobody has ever had to move a row back, and this spring, for the first time, the grey has come in past the new row at night and gone back by day.
encounter: at night the grey comes in over the rows, and what walks in it walks with it
hook: The newest row's knots have been tied again in the night, in grey rush, by somebody who knew the weave.

name: The Name-Wife's Hollow
unique_feature: a cave at the foot of the South Scarp at the head of a gully where the scarp curls round a cove, the mouth a cleft in the scarp's rock with a thread of water weeping off its cheek, a bog-oak beam before the mouth hung with knotted cords, and before it a dead sallow hung so thick with them that from the delta it reads as a grey cloud against the scarp
story: The marsh-hag the reedfolk call the Name-Wife cures anything: a fever, the cough that comes off the flats in autumn, a child that will not turn. She takes in payment a name you know, never your own, and she knots it into a cord of rush and hangs it in her hollow under the South Scarp, and the one whose name it was begins, slowly, to be forgotten: their place at the table not laid, their lantern not lit, their boat called by somebody else's name. The reedfolk go to her anyway. The cords hang from every branch of the dead sallow in her cove and in curtains down the walls of the hollow, and Nauvissa says there are more names under the scarp than there are in Isseva.
encounter: her leech-hounds lie up in the cove by day and wisps hang over the weep-pool at night; inside, the hounds' den, the forgotten she keeps, and the Name-Wife herself at the back of the hollow, knotting
hook: The cords on the beam across the mouth are new this spring, and one of them is knotted in the Nauve weave.

name: The Sounding
unique_feature: a tower of black bog-oak twenty metres tall raised by the Flood-Callers on a drowned Builders' platform in a mere on the North Shore, a stair of four flights climbing round its outside to a railed deck, a great bell hung under its hood and cut burial lanterns strung round the eaves; the door into the platform's undercroft at its back
story: The Builders left a platform of fused black stone on the North Shore with a ring-wall round it, and the marsh came up over the wall and stopped at the platform's lip. The Flood-Callers have raised a tower on it, of bog-oak dragged out of the peat, and hung a bell in it they cast from the brass hooks of a thousand burial lanterns. They mean to ring it at the spring tide, from below: the bell-rope runs down through the tower and the platform into the well in the undercroft, where the black water is, and the drowned are. They call the tower the Sounding, which in Sedgish is also the word for measuring how deep the water is.
encounter: Flood-Callers on the bell deck and Ebb-Hands at their camp by the steps; at night the drowned they keep in the mere come up round the platform; below, the Callers' choir and the Sounder at the well
hook: Cut up the tower's first leg are tide-marks, one for every spring tide since the Callers came, each higher than the last; the top one is level with the bell.

name: The Saltgate
unique_feature: a square Tollmere fort of grey ashlar on the headland at the Outfall's mouth, its keep standing over the Guild's great sluice where the channel meets the sea; the sea-gates hang open, the yard is standing water and weed, and on its walls the garrison still keeps the watch, drowned
story: The Tallymen's Guild built the Saltgate to hold the sea out of the Outfall and drain the Delta behind it, field by field, for Tollmere: a fort on the headland and under it the culverts and the great sluice, the gates shut at the flood and opened at the ebb by a windlass in the keep. Last autumn something came up the culverts from the sea side at the spring tide and broke the gates from below. The sea came in through the undercroft in the night with the garrison asleep in it. They are still at their posts. The reedfolk on the south bank say the gates have hung open ever since, and that the eels came back to the Outfall that same week.
encounter: the drowned garrison keeps the walls and the gate; wisps burn on the towers where the beacons were; below, in the flooded culverts, the drowned and the sallowjaws that came up the sluice, and in the sump Old Mudmouth
hook: The Guild's last order is still nailed to the gate, swollen with salt: the sluice to be shut at the flood, on pain of the Guild's displeasure; under it somebody has chalked a reedfolk knot that means leave it.

site.hook_prompt: Read the notices on the gate

name: The Flood-Bride
unique_feature: a bride of bound reed and withy three times a man's height standing at the edge of a black mere with her arms held out over the water, an indigo veil streaming from her crown to the ground and her hem knotted thick with cords; last spring's bride slumped grey into the water beside her, and on the bank the weavers' withy frame where next spring's is already begun
story: Every spring the Bride-Weavers of Isseva bind a bride of reed and walk her out to the mere north of the town to be married to the flood, so that it keeps to the sea one more year: the Tide is a shore, they say, and a shore must be courted. Mother Orrin Vasse has woven forty brides. This spring's bride was found one morning turned on her own feet to face the land, and since then the drowned have come up out of the mere at dark and stood before her in rows, like guests at a wedding.
encounter: after dark the drowned wade up out of the mere and stand in rows before the Bride like guests; they turn on whoever stands between them and her
hook: One cord in the Bride's hem is tied in no weave the weavers know, and it is wet to the knot though the hem hangs a yard above the water.

name: The Wisp-Catcher's Rack
unique_feature: a gallows-frame of bog-oak twice a man's height and twelve paces long hung with forty glass jars on cords, each with a wisp in it burning cold green, so that from the causeway at night the rack reads as a hanging cloud of small lights; under it more jars waiting in a row, and beside it the catcher's stilt-hut, his long-handled nets and his bench of empty jars
story: Ferrit Oache catches wisps. He goes out on the North Fen at the dark of the moon with a net of eel-skin and a jar of salt water, and he comes home with lights that never want oil, and Isseva's lantern-wrights pay him in silver and do not ask what they are. They are not lanterns. The reedfolk say a wisp is what goes out of a drowned man when his burial lantern does. Ferrit says he has never caught one that spoke. Lately the wild ones come in to the rack at night and drift round the jars, and the jarred ones dim while they are there.
encounter: the wild wisps come in off the fen after dark and drift round the rack; the jarred ones dim while they are there
hook: One jar at the end of the rack is cracked and empty, and its cord is knotted in the Lissa weave.

name: The Flood-Mark
unique_feature: a needle of the Builders' black stone four storeys tall on a stepped plinth at the channel's edge, cut round near its top with one line that the spray has filled white, and lashed up its face a white timber gauge notched for every spring tide in Sedgemire's memory, every notch far below the Builders' line; a ladder up its side to a railed seat, a pennant at its head, a float-well at its foot and the tide-watcher's stilt-hut on the bank
story: The Builders cut one line round the needle, high up, and nobody knows what it marks. The Tide-Watchers of Oulea say it is the flood: the height the water stood at once, and will stand at again when the Dwindling turns and the sea comes back for what it left. For two hundred years one of them has sat at the needle's foot and notched the gauge at every spring tide. Hesk Vaurel is the last. She says the notches have been climbing, a finger's breadth in a lifetime, and that she has started to sleep in her boots.
encounter: a sallowjaw lies up on the plinth's lowest step at the ebb, where the float-well's eels come to it
hook: Above the highest notch on the gauge somebody has cut a new one, a hand's breadth higher, and it is not in Hesk's hand.

name: Hask's Ropewalk
unique_feature: a ropewalk sixty paces long laid dead straight across a peat island: at its head a great wheel under a reed lean-to, down its length a file of T-headed trestles carrying three pale strands, at its foot the weighted sledge that walks as the rope is laid; eel-skins and reed drying on lines beside it, coils of finished rope, a tar-pot smoking, and a rack of ropes each tied with an indigo rag
story: Every rope in Isseva that holds a boat, a boardwalk or a burial lantern was walked at Hask's: three strands of reed-hemp and one of eel-skin, laid by the Hasks for six generations. Into every one, by the old custom, a name is walked: the walker says it at the wheel as the twist goes in, and the rope holds the name the way it holds a boat. The rack at the head is the ropes waiting for their buyers. Corra Hask walks them now. One rope on the rack nobody has come for in nine years, and it has her brother's name in it.
encounter: by day Corra Hask walks the strands with the wheel turning at the head; nothing hunts the island but the herons
hook: On the rack of named ropes one has hung so long that its rag has gone grey, and its tag says 'for Iven Hask, when he comes home'.

name: The Unwinding
unique_feature: a round maze of reed hedges a man's height and thirty paces across, its one path winding five times round on itself to a black pool at the middle with a flat grey stone beside it; over the pool a pole seven metres tall crowned with a wheel of reed and hung with the ribbons every walker has tied, and at its single gate two posts hung with knotted cords
story: The reedfolk say grief is a rope that has to be unwound the way it was wound, and the Unwinding is where Nauvissa goes to do it: you walk in with the thing you cannot say, five times round, and you say it at the pool where nobody hears but the water, and you walk out the same way with your hands empty. Edda Moye has kept the hedges trimmed for fifty years and has never once walked it herself. She says she is saving it.
encounter: after dark a wisp hangs over the middle pool and will not be led out
hook: Of all the ribbons on the pole one is not cloth but a cord of rush knotted in a family's weave, the way the Name-Wife ties hers.

name: The Grey Heronry
unique_feature: a stand of nine dead alders drowned to the knee in a black pool, their crowns heaped with the herons' great stick nests and whitewashed with their droppings, a grey bird standing on every nest and more wading at the edge; on the bank a heron-reader's hide on short stilts with a slate by its door chalked with flights
story: The herons of the North Fen have nested in the dead alders by the Nave since before the Nave leaned, and the reedfolk read them: which way the flight goes up at dawn, how many, whether they come back. Pell Oduin has read them for the Reed Council for thirty years from his hide on the bank, and the Council does as he says, mostly. He reads for anyone who will sit with him. He says the herons always know where something new has come into the fen, because they go to look at it.
encounter: sallowjaws lie in the black pool under the nests by day, waiting for a chick to fall
hook: The slate by the hide's door has this morning's flight chalked on it, and under it, in Pell's hand: 'all of them west, to the old water, and only half came back'.

name: The Sundew Garden
unique_feature: raised beds of black peat in rows under hoops of withy, planted with sundews as broad as a cartwheel glistening red with dew and pitcher-plants standing knee-high; over them a pole seven metres tall with a wicker cage of eel-heads at its top, smoking with flies; and in a sunken tub by the herb-wife's hut the Mother Sundew, as wide across as a boat
story: Nelle Saye grows what the marsh grows, bigger. Her sundews' dew is the glue Isseva's lantern-wrights set their horn panes with, the bleeders' best salve, and in a weak dose a sleep without dreams. The Mother Sundew in the tub by her door is older than Nelle and was her grandmother's; it is fed an eel a week, and lately it has started to close on the eel before the eel is dropped.
encounter: wisps come to the fly-tower after dark, and the flies go quiet while they are there
hook: On the rim of the Mother Sundew's tub there is a boot, only a boot, its laces still tied.

name: The Great Dredge
unique_feature: a Tollmere dredging-crane as tall as a tower beached on its stone-laden barge at the channel's edge: a treadwheel the height of two men on the deck, a pair of sheer-legs nineteen metres tall leaning out over the black square shaft the Guild cut through the peat, its bucket-chain hanging stiff from their head down into the dark, and the timber head-frame over the shaft's mouth with its ladder going down
story: The Tallymen's Guild means to drain the Delta for Tollmere, field by field, and this spring its engineers found under the peat west of Isseva what the Builders left there: a street of black stone eight metres down, doorways off it, and a hall. They brought the Great Dredge up the channel to dig it out and cut a shaft. Brannoc Tull was the dredge-master. Three weeks ago the crew went down at the change of shift and nobody came up, and the treadwheel has not turned since, and at night the bucket-chain has been heard to move on its own, link by link, as if something below were climbing it.
encounter: the drowned crew stand their shift at the shaft-head after dark; below, in the Guild's cuttings and the Builders' drowned street, the crew and what came up to meet them, and the dredge-master at the bottom of the shaft
hook: The crew's tally-board hangs by the shaft with every man's peg pushed in to 'below', and none out.

name: The Keel-Barrow
unique_feature: a long turf barrow on the tideflats' last dry ground with the stem and stern of a great ship standing out of either end, each a black oak post twice a man's height curling over at the top into a gull's head; her grey clinker strakes showing where the turf has slumped, her crew's oars stood upright along her ridge, the stump of her mast hung with a sail of rusted chain, and in her side a door of salt-white boards
story: When the Salt Isles still traded up the Delta their sea-kings were buried in their ships, and one king who died in Sedgemire was buried here: his ship dragged up the flats and sunk in the last dry ground and turfed over, his crew laid at their oars inside her. The reedfolk say the Salt Isles did it so the sea would have to come inland to fetch him. Lately the barrow's stem has been moving, a finger's breadth a night, turning toward the sea, and the drowned of the Outfall come up the flats in the dark and stand at her side as if waiting to be taken aboard.
encounter: the drowned come up the flats after dark and wait at the barrow's side like a crew mustering; inside, the king's oarsmen at their benches, sallowjaws in the flooded hold, and the Keel-King at his steering-oar
hook: Somebody has tied a mooring-rope to the ring-bolt in the stem-post, and the rope runs out across the flats toward the sea, taut.

site.hook_prompt: Look at the mooring-rope on the stake
